title: Knowledge check: Security Auditing of Legacy ASP Applications

questions.prompt: Which subtopic is explicitly listed under “Security Auditing of Legacy ASP Applications” in the attached Classic ASP curriculum?
questions.explanation: The PDF lists “Inventorying entry points” under lesson 100, “Security Auditing of Legacy ASP Applications”. The distractors belong to other lesson topics.

questions.prompt: When applying “Security Auditing of Legacy ASP Applications” in a legacy Classic ASP application, which approach is strongest?
options: Enforce the control on the server and verify a denial/failure case.
Hide the button but leave the endpoint unprotected.
Return internal diagnostics to every browser.
questions.answer_key: Enforce the control on the server and verify a denial/failure case.
questions.explanation: This approach keeps security auditing of legacy asp applications testable and respects Classic ASP/IIS runtime boundaries. The exact IIS, provider, or component behavior must be checked in the target test environment.

questions.prompt: Before marking work on “Security Auditing of Legacy ASP Applications” ready for review, what evidence should be recorded?
options: Claim the production deployment passed without running it.
Delete diagnostic evidence before recording the outcome.
Treat a successful happy-path test as proof of all security properties.
Document the observed result, tool/runtime version, and one meaningful failure or edge case.
questions.answer_key: Document the observed result, tool/runtime version, and one meaningful failure or edge case.
questions.explanation: Good maintenance evidence includes the expected and observed result, relevant version/runtime assumptions, and a boundary or failure test. Never claim an execution/deployment test that was not run.
